entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Of a person: very tired or exhausted, especially after work or physical effort (*I'm beat*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech, mostly in the short phrase *I'm beat* at the end of a long day. It's informal but not slang, and it only works after verbs like *be*, *feel* or *look*, never before a noun (*a beat person* is wrong). Fine with family and coworkers, but not in formal writing.
examples: I've been on my feet all day at the store, and I'm **beat**.
You look **beat**. Sit down and I'll make dinner tonight.
After moving all that furniture, we were too **beat** to go out.

drill.sentence: We drove eleven hours straight to get to Grandma's, and by the time we pulled in, we were {{beat}}.
drill.hint: out of energy after a long day (one word; not *dead*, *tired*, *wiped* or *exhausted*)

entries.related: *wiped (out)* — same, also informal; *worn out* — neutral; *beat-up* — old and damaged (*a beat-up car*), a different meaning.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Extremely busy, with too much work or too many customers at once.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, especially in restaurants, retail and busy offices, and among younger workers. It often suggests a sudden rush (*We got slammed at lunch*), while *swamped* is more about a pile of work. Fine in friendly work chat (*I'm slammed today, can we do Thursday?*), but not in formal writing.
examples: The diner got **slammed** right after the parade, and we ran out of pancakes.
I'm totally **slammed** this week; can we push our call to Monday?
Tax season is brutal; my mom's accounting office is **slammed** every April.

drill.sentence: The coffee shop was {{slammed}} this morning, with a line out the door until ten.
drill.hint: hit by a huge rush of customers (not *swamped*, *packed* or *busy*)

entries.related: *swamped* — overloaded with work; *buried* — informal, too much work to get through; *dead* — the opposite, no customers at all.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Mentally exhausted, so tired that you can no longer think clearly or focus.
entries.usage: Slang used mostly by students and younger office workers, often in *My brain is fried* or *I'm completely fried*. It's about mental tiredness from studying, screens or stress, not from physical work. Fine with friends and friendly coworkers, but too casual for an email to your manager.
examples: After eight hours of exams, my brain is completely **fried**.
I've been staring at spreadsheets since seven, and I'm **fried**.
By the end of the six-hour drive, the kids were **fried**, and honestly, so were we.

drill.sentence: Can we do the crossword tomorrow? My brain is {{fried}} after all that tax paperwork.
drill.hint: too worn out to think (slang; not *mush*, *toast* or *dead*)

entries.related: *burned out* — exhausted from long-term stress, more serious; *brain-dead* — informal, too tired to think; *beat* — physically tired.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very excited and eager about something that is going to happen.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech and fine with friendly coworkers, but not in formal writing. The *p* is silent: /saɪkt/. Use *psyched about* / *for* + noun or *psyched to* + verb; *psyched up* means mentally ready for a challenge.
entries.pattern: psyched about / for + noun; psyched to + verb
examples: My daughter is so **psyched** about her first sleepover that she packed a week early.
We're **psyched** to finally have a backyard where the dog can run around.
I was **psyched** for the game until I saw the forecast: rain all afternoon.

drill.sentence: Honestly, I'm {{psyched}} about the new bike trail; it goes right past our house.
drill.hint: really looking forward to it (silent first letter; not *stoked*, *pumped*, *hyped* or *excited*)

entries.related: *psyched out* — made nervous or scared by someone; *stoked* — same, more slangy; *pumped* — excited and full of energy.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Very excited and happy about something, either coming up or just happened.
entries.usage: Slang associated with California surf culture, now used across the US, mostly by younger and middle-aged speakers: *I'm so stoked!* Use *stoked about* / *for* + noun or *stoked to* + verb. It sounds happy and laid-back, and it's fine with friends and casual coworkers but not in formal writing.
examples: We just heard back about the apartment, and we got it! I'm so **stoked**.
The kids were **stoked** when they woke up to snow on Saturday morning.
My dad was **stoked** when his old high school team finally won the state title.

drill.sentence: My best friend is moving back to town next month, and I'm {{stoked}}!
drill.hint: beyond happy about it (surfer slang; not *psyched*, *pumped*, *thrilled* or *excited*)

entries.related: *psyched* — very close; *thrilled* — neutral and stronger; *hyped* — slang, excited, often about something new.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person or thing that spoils other people's fun or good mood.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans in casual talk and texts: *Don't be such a buzzkill.* It's used about people who bring up rules or bad news, and about events like rain or an early closing time. Often said jokingly, but calling someone *a buzzkill* is still a criticism, so keep it among friends.
examples: I hate to be **a buzzkill**, but we have to leave by ten to catch the last bus.
The rain was a total **buzzkill**; the whole festival moved into one crowded tent.
My uncle is such **a buzzkill**; he talks about his cholesterol at every family dinner.

drill.sentence: Every time we start having fun, he reminds us about work on Monday. He's such a {{buzzkill}}.
drill.hint: someone who spoils the fun (slang; not *killjoy*, *downer* or *party pooper*)

entries.related: *killjoy* — same meaning, older and less slangy; *party pooper* — playful, a bit childish; *wet blanket* — idiom, someone who spoils fun.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A small, specific habit or thing that annoys you much more than it probably should.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation and casual writing, often as *one of my pet peeves is…* or *my biggest pet peeve*. It's about small everyday annoyances, not serious problems, and it's fine in light talk with coworkers. British speakers usually say *pet hate* instead.
examples: My biggest **pet peeve** is people who stop right at the top of the escalator.
One of my **pet peeves** at work is meetings that could have been an email.
Loud chewing is my mom's **pet peeve**, so we all eat very quietly at her house.

drill.sentence: Leaving wet towels on the bed is my husband's biggest {{pet peeve}}; it drives him crazy.
drill.hint: small thing that annoys someone a lot (not *pet hate* or *complaint*)

entries.related: *pet hate* — British equivalent; *a sore point* — a topic that upsets someone; *a nuisance* — something annoying, neutral.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: In casual speech: odd and unexpected, or unknown and unimportant (*some random guy*), rather than chosen by chance.
entries.usage: Very common in casual speech, especially among younger people, in *That was so random* and *some random guy*. In formal writing, *random* keeps its standard meaning, *by chance* (*a random sample*). *Some random* + person sounds a bit dismissive: the person is a stranger who doesn't matter.
examples: Some **random** guy at the gas station started telling me about his divorce.
My aunt sent me a **random** text at 2 a.m. asking if I like pickles.
That was such a **random** thing to say in the middle of a job interview.

drill.sentence: We were talking about the weather, and out of nowhere he asked about my shoe size. So {{random}}.
drill.hint: strangely unexpected, unconnected to anything (not *weird*, *odd* or *strange*)

entries.related: *out of nowhere* — unexpectedly; *weird* — strange in general; *at random* — by chance, standard.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Slightly wrong, strange or not normal, in a way that is hard to name (*Something feels off*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and fine at work: *The numbers look a little off.* It follows *be, look, seem, feel, sound* and is often softened with *a little* or *kind of*. About food and milk it means starting to go bad (*The milk smells off*).
examples: I can't explain it, but something about his story felt **off**.
The colors in the photo look a little **off**; maybe the camera settings were wrong.
Jake seemed **off** at dinner; I hope everything's okay with him.

drill.sentence: The house was quiet when we got home, and the back door was open. Something was definitely {{off}}.
drill.hint: strange in a way that's hard to name (one word; not *wrong*, *weird* or *up*)

entries.related: *not right* — similar, more direct; *fishy* — suspicious, suggesting dishonesty; *something's up* — something unusual is happening.

entries.label: adverb
entries.meaning: Very or extremely, used before adjectives and adverbs (*super helpful*, *super easy*).
entries.usage: Very common in casual American speech, especially among younger adults, and it appears in friendly work emails too (*super helpful, thanks!*). It goes before adjectives and adverbs, sounds upbeat and friendly, and is informal rather than slang. In formal writing, use *very* or *extremely* instead.
examples: That video on fixing a leaky faucet was **super** helpful; I did it in ten minutes.
The hike was **super** easy, even for my eighty-year-old grandpa.
I'm **super** sorry I'm late; the bus broke down.

drill.sentence: The new coffee place downtown is {{super}} cute, and the pastries are amazing.
drill.hint: upbeat, casual intensifier (not *really*, *so*, *pretty* or *very*)

entries.related: *really* / *so* — equally casual; *very* — neutral, fine in writing; *extremely* — stronger and more neutral.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: A lot or a large amount: *a ton of* + noun, or *a ton* after a verb (*I learned a ton*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and friendly emails: *a ton of emails*, *thanks a ton*. *Tons of* means the same. With a plural noun the verb is plural (*A ton of people were there*), and in formal writing *a great deal of* or *many* fits better.
examples: I came back from vacation to **a ton of** emails and two angry voicemails.
Thanks **a ton** for watching the kids; we really needed a night out.
There's **a ton of** construction downtown right now, so leave early.

drill.sentence: My grandma always cooks {{a ton of}} food for Thanksgiving, so we eat leftovers for a week.
drill.hint: a huge amount of, informally (a unit of weight; not *a lot of*, *tons of* or *loads of*)

entries.related: *tons of* — same; *a lot of* — neutral; *loads of* — informal, more common in British English.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: People in general, said in a friendly way; *my folks* means your parents or family.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in American speech; *Okay, folks* is a warm way for teachers, guides or pilots to address a group. *My folks* usually means your parents. It sounds friendly and down-to-earth, but in formal writing say *people* or *parents*.
examples: I'm visiting my **folks** in Ohio for Thanksgiving.
Okay, **folks**, let's take our seats; the show starts in five minutes.
A lot of **folks** in this town worked at the old furniture factory their whole lives.

drill.sentence: I'm going home this weekend because my {{folks}} want help cleaning out the garage.
drill.hint: the people who raised me (informal; not *parents* or *family*)

entries.related: *parents* — neutral; *you folks* — friendly way to address a group, like *you guys*; *people* — neutral.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A man or guy; also a casual way to address someone, or a one-word reaction of surprise (*Dude!*).
entries.usage: Very common in American speech, especially among younger men, but also used by women and older people with friends. It can mean *a guy* (*some dude*), address a friend (*Dude, look at this*) or, on its own, show surprise or annoyance (*Dude!*). Never use it with a boss, a client or a stranger in a formal setting.
examples: Some **dude** in the parking lot helped me jump-start my car.
My sister's new boyfriend seems like a pretty chill **dude**; we talked about fishing for an hour.
**Dude**, you ate my leftovers! I was saving those.

drill.sentence: My brother answered the phone with "{{Dude}}, where are you? The game started ten minutes ago!"
drill.hint: casual word to address a friend (slang; not *man*, *bro* or *hey*)

entries.related: *guy* — informal, neutral for a man; *bro* — slang, more masculine; *man* — also used to address someone (*Come on, man*).

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Boring, weak or unconvincing; not cool or not good enough (*a lame excuse*, *a lame party*).
entries.usage: Common in casual speech, especially among teens and younger adults: *That's so lame.* *A lame excuse* is used by everyone and is only mildly informal. Some people avoid the word because its original meaning, *unable to walk normally*, refers to a disability.
examples: He said he was late because his cat was sick, which is a pretty **lame** excuse.
The party was kind of **lame**, so we left early and got burgers.
Their new logo is so **lame**; it looks like clip art from the nineties.

drill.sentence: "Sorry, I can't come; I need to wash my hair." "That's the {{lamest}} excuse I've ever heard."
drill.hint: least convincing (superlative; not *worst*, *weakest* or *dumbest*)

entries.related: *weak* — neutral, about excuses and arguments; *boring* — neutral; *cool* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To annoy or bother someone, either a little at a time or by something that keeps coming back to mind.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and fine with coworkers: *It really bugs me when people are late.* The subject is often *it* or *what* (*What bugs me is…*). It can also mean to keep asking someone for something (*Stop bugging me about the dishes*).
examples: It really **bugs** me when people leave their shopping carts in the parking lot.
Stop **bugging** your sister; she's trying to do her homework.
What **bugs** me about the new office is that there's nowhere quiet to make a call.

drill.sentence: My dad's been {{bugging}} me to call my grandmother, so I finally did yesterday.
drill.hint: annoyingly and repeatedly asking (not *asking*, *nagging* or *pestering*)

entries.related: *annoy* — neutral; *get on someone's nerves* — informal, annoy a lot; *nag* — keep criticizing or reminding.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To get a quick, casual meal or snack, often together with someone.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech and in friendly invitations to coworkers: *Want to grab a bite after this?* It suggests something simple and quick, not a formal dinner. *Grab a bite to eat* is the longer form, and *grab lunch* or *grab coffee* follow the same pattern.
examples: We have an hour before the movie; want to **grab a bite** across the street?
Let's **grab a bite** after the meeting and talk it through.
On road trips, we usually **grab a bite** at whatever diner is near the exit.

drill.sentence: I'm starving. Do you have time to {{grab a bite}} before your train leaves?
drill.hint: have a quick, casual meal (three words; not *eat* or *get some food*)

entries.related: *grab a bite to eat* — same; *get something to eat* — neutral; *a bite* — a small amount of food.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To watch many episodes of a TV show one after another, often a whole season in one or two sittings.
entries.usage: Used by all ages since streaming became normal, in speech and in the media: *We binge-watched the whole series.* It's informal but not slang, so news articles use it freely. People also say just *binge* (*I binged it in a weekend*) and use *binge-watching* as a noun.
examples: We **binge-watched** the entire first season last weekend and barely left the couch.
When I'm sick, I just stay in bed and **binge-watch** old sitcoms.
Streaming services release whole seasons at once because they know people will **binge-watch** them.

drill.sentence: My plan for the snow day is simple: stay in my pajamas and {{binge-watch}} that new crime drama.
drill.hint: view episode after episode in one go (hyphenated; not *stream*)

entries.related: *binge* — the short verb; *marathon* — a long session of one show; *stream* — watch online, neutral.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Extremely impressed or amazed by something, often more than you expected.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, reviews and friendly work emails, and it's always positive: *We were blown away by your work.* It's usually passive with *by*, but the active form is common too (*Her performance blew me away*). It's informal but not slang.
entries.pattern: be / get blown away by + noun; something blows someone away
examples: I'd seen photos, but I was still **blown away** by the Grand Canyon in person.
The judges were **blown away** by a twelve-year-old who played Chopin from memory.
Honestly, the food at that tiny place **blew us away**.

drill.sentence: I didn't expect much from the school play, but I was {{blown away}} by how well the kids sang.
drill.hint: hugely impressed (two words; not *amazed*, *floored*, *stunned* or *impressed*)

entries.related: *floored* — so surprised you can't react; *impressed* — neutral and weaker; *mind-blowing* — adjective, amazing.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: Not fully alert or aware, because you are tired, sick, on medication or distracted.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, often to explain why you're slow or forgetful: *Sorry, I'm a little out of it today.* It's fine with coworkers in conversation, but not in formal writing. The cause often comes with *from* or *after*: *still out of it from the anesthesia*.
examples: Sorry if I seem **out of it**; the baby was up all night.
He was still pretty **out of it** after the surgery, so we kept the visit short.
I was so **out of it** this morning that I poured orange juice into my cereal.

drill.sentence: The cold medicine made me so {{out of it}} that I almost missed my bus stop.
drill.hint: not fully alert (three words; not *groggy*, *drowsy* or *spacey*)

entries.related: *groggy* — tired and confused, often after sleep; *spaced out* — not paying attention; *with it* — the opposite, alert (*I'm not very with it today*).

entries.label: slang
entries.meaning: Finished, ruined or in serious trouble, especially if something goes wrong (*If we miss this deadline, we're toast*).
entries.usage: Slang used by Americans of most ages, usually after *be*: *you're toast*, *we're toast*, *my laptop is toast*. It often sounds half-joking, a dramatic way to describe a bad outcome. Fine among friends and casual coworkers, but too casual for written work communication.
examples: If Mom finds out we used her car, we're **toast**.
I dropped my phone in the lake, so it's definitely **toast**.
One more injury and the team's season is **toast**.

drill.sentence: If the landlord sees the dog, we're {{toast}}; pets aren't allowed in this building.
drill.hint: in really big trouble (slang, one word; not *dead*, *done*, *screwed* or *busted*)

entries.related: *done for* — informal, finished; *dead meat* — slang, in serious trouble; *in hot water* — idiom, in trouble.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Caught doing something wrong or forbidden; also, very informally, broken (*a busted phone*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech: *You're busted!* or *We got busted.* In news writing, *busted for* + crime means arrested. The *broken* sense is very casual and American (*a busted zipper*, *the AC is busted*).
examples: My little brother got **busted** sneaking cookies before dinner.
Two teenagers were **busted** for spray-painting the bridge last night.
The elevator in our building has been **busted** for a week, and we live on the sixth floor.

drill.sentence: We tried to sneak into a second movie without a ticket, but we got {{busted}} by an usher.
drill.hint: found out in the act (not *caught* or *nabbed*)

entries.related: *caught* — neutral; *caught red-handed* — caught in the act; *broken* — neutral for the second sense.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Poorly made, unreliable or likely to break; working badly in a way that looks improvised.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans, gamers and programmers, about cars, apartments, tools, apps and quick fixes. It's often affectionate about your own things and critical about other people's. The noun is *jank*, and both are too casual for formal writing or emails to clients.
examples: My first car was so **janky** that the passenger door only opened from the outside.
The hotel Wi-Fi is really **janky**; it drops every ten minutes.
We fixed the shelf with tape and a coat hanger; it's **janky**, but it works.

drill.sentence: The ladder looked so {{janky}} that I refused to climb past the second step.
drill.hint: badly made and unreliable (slang; not *sketchy*, *rickety*, *wobbly* or *shaky*)

entries.related: *sketchy* — suspicious or unsafe; *rickety* — old and likely to collapse, neutral; *jury-rigged* — fixed in a temporary, improvised way.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Uncertain or doubtful; also of questionable quality, so you're not sure you can trust it.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech about plans, weather, food, health and quality: *The weather looks iffy.* It sounds milder than *sketchy*: something is uncertain, not necessarily dangerous. Fine with coworkers (*The numbers are a bit iffy*), but not in formal writing.
examples: The forecast looks **iffy** for Saturday, so let's have a backup plan for the picnic.
That sushi smelled a little **iffy**, so I didn't eat it.
Whether he'll be ready for the playoffs is still **iffy** after his knee injury.

drill.sentence: I'd love to come to your party, but it's a bit {{iffy}}; I might have to work that night.
drill.hint: hard to say for sure (not *uncertain*, *unclear* or *up in the air*)

entries.related: *sketchy* — suspicious or unsafe; *up in the air* — not decided yet; *dicey* — risky and uncertain.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person or situation in complete disorder: disorganized, chaotic or emotionally all over the place.
entries.usage: Slang common among younger Americans, often used about yourself with humor: *I'm a hot mess today.* About others it can be affectionate or critical. It's fine for joking with friendly coworkers, but too casual for work writing.
examples: I overslept, spilled coffee on my shirt and forgot my keys; I'm **a hot mess** today.
The airport was **a hot mess**: delayed flights, long lines and nobody at the help desk.
After the breakup, he was kind of **a hot mess** for a few weeks.

drill.sentence: The kitchen is {{a hot mess}} after the kids tried to bake a birthday cake by themselves.
drill.hint: total chaos (slang, three words; not *a disaster* or *a dumpster fire*)

entries.related: *a mess* — neutral; *a dumpster fire* — a disastrous situation that keeps getting worse; *a train wreck* — a complete failure, often a person.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A chaotic, disastrous situation that keeps getting worse and that nobody seems able to fix.
entries.usage: Slang that became widespread in American media and online in the mid-2010s, used by younger and middle-aged speakers in conversation and in casual journalism about failed events, projects or sports seasons. It's stronger than *a hot mess* and usually describes situations, not people. Avoid it in formal writing and in front of the people responsible.
examples: The company picnic was **a dumpster fire**: the caterer never showed up, and then it poured.
Their season has been **a total dumpster fire**; they've lost eleven games in a row.
The software update was **a dumpster fire**, and half the app stopped working.

drill.sentence: Our group project turned into {{a dumpster fire}} when two people quit and the deadline moved up.
drill.hint: chaos that keeps getting worse (slang; not *a disaster*, *a hot mess* or *a train wreck*)

entries.related: *a train wreck* — a disaster you can't stop watching; *a hot mess* — chaotic, often a person; *a fiasco* — neutral, a complete failure.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To be less strict or critical with someone, because their situation is difficult or they are trying their best.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in American conversation, often as a request on someone's behalf: *Cut him some slack, it's his first week.* It sounds kind and fair-minded, and *cut yourself some slack* means to stop being so hard on yourself. Fine with coworkers in speech, but too casual for formal writing.
examples: **Cut her some slack**; she's only been driving for a month.
My boss **cut me some slack** on the deadline because my dad was in the hospital.
You've been working nonstop; **cut yourself some slack** and take the weekend off.

drill.sentence: He forgot your birthday, but he's had a terrible month, so maybe {{cut him some slack}}.
drill.hint: be more forgiving with him, as an idiom (not *go easy on him* or *give him a break*)

entries.related: *go easy on someone* — same, slightly more neutral; *give someone a break* — similar, also *stop criticizing*; *give someone the benefit of the doubt* — assume they meant well.

entries.label: spoken phrase
entries.meaning: Don't worry about it; it's not a problem. Used to reassure someone or to reply to an apology or thanks.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech as a relaxed reply to *sorry* or *thank you*. A related saying is *Don't sweat the small stuff* (don't worry about minor problems). Fine with coworkers in speech and chat, but too casual for formal emails.
examples: "Sorry I spilled wine on your rug." "**Don't sweat it**; it'll come out."
If you can't make it to practice, **don't sweat it**. We'll catch you up next week.
"Thanks for covering my shift." "**Don't sweat it**, you'd do the same for me."

drill.sentence: "I feel terrible that you had to drive all the way out here to get me." "{{Don't sweat it}}. It was on my way home."
drill.hint: relax, it's no problem (three words; not *no worries* or *no big deal*)

entries.related: *no worries* — very common casual reply; *don't worry about it* — neutral; *it's all good* — slang, everything is fine.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To accept something unpleasant or difficult without complaining, and just deal with it.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech, often as blunt advice from coaches, parents or friends: *Suck it up, it's only one more mile.* Said to someone else it can sound harsh or unsympathetic, but about yourself it's fine (*I just sucked it up*). Some people find it rude, so keep it out of work emails.
examples: The flight was delayed six hours, so we just **sucked it up** and found a place to eat.
I hate going to the dentist, but I **suck it up** twice a year.
"It's freezing out here." "**Suck it up**; we're almost at the car."

drill.sentence: The job pays well, so I'll {{suck it up}} and live with the long commute for a year.
drill.hint: accept the bad part without complaining (not *tough it out* or *grin and bear it*)

entries.related: *tough it out* — keep going through something hard; *grin and bear it* — accept something unpleasant calmly; *deal with it* — informal, accept it.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To stop being so serious, strict or worried, and relax a little.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, usually as an imperative: *Lighten up, it's just a game.* It can sound dismissive, as if the other person is overreacting, so be careful with people who are really upset. *Lighten up on someone* means to be less strict with them.
entries.pattern: lighten up; lighten up on someone
examples: **Lighten up**! It was just a joke, and nobody got hurt.
My parents finally **lightened up** about curfew when I turned seventeen.
You might want to **lighten up** on the new hires; they're still learning.

drill.sentence: It's a board game, not the Olympics. {{Lighten up}} and have some fun!
drill.hint: a two-word order to relax and not take things so seriously (not *chill out* or *loosen up*)

entries.related: *chill out* — calm down, slang; *loosen up* — become less stiff or formal; *lighten the mood* — make a situation less serious.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To relax completely and do nothing that needs effort, for example lying on the couch watching TV.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, often with *in front of the TV* or *on the couch*. *Veg* is short for *vegetate* and is pronounced like the start of *vegetable*. It's usually about rest you've earned, not a criticism, but it's too casual for formal writing.
examples: After finals, I just want to **veg out** on the couch for a week.
Sunday is our day to **veg out**: pajamas, pancakes and old movies.
The kids **vegged out** in front of the TV while we cleaned up after the party.

drill.sentence: I'm not going anywhere tonight; I'm just going to {{veg out}} and watch cartoons.
drill.hint: do nothing at all, lazily (not *chill out*, *kick back* or *relax*)

entries.related: *chill (out)* — relax, slang; *lounge around* — relax lazily; *couch potato* — a person who watches a lot of TV.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Of food or drink: to be exactly what you needed or wanted at that moment.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech after eating or drinking something satisfying: *That really hit the spot.* The subject is the food or drink, not the person. It's warm and informal but not slang, and it works best with simple things like soup, coffee or a sandwich.
examples: That bowl of hot soup really **hit the spot** after shoveling snow all morning.
A cold lemonade would **hit the spot** right now.
Thanks for the sandwich; it totally **hit the spot**.

drill.sentence: We'd been hiking for five hours, so those burgers at the end really {{hit the spot}}.
drill.hint: were exactly what we needed (not *did the trick*)

entries.related: *do the trick* — work or solve a problem; *just what the doctor ordered* — exactly what was needed, humorous; *satisfying* — neutral.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Restless and impatient, unable to sit still, often while waiting for something.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech about kids on long trips, people waiting for news, or anyone stuck inside: *The kids are getting antsy.* It often goes with *get* or *a little*. It describes restlessness, not deep anxiety, and it's too casual for formal writing.
examples: The kids got **antsy** after two hours in the car, so we stopped at a playground.
I always get **antsy** waiting for test results from the doctor.
After a week of rain, the dog was **antsy** and kept bringing us his leash.

drill.sentence: My grandpa hates waiting rooms; after ten minutes he gets {{antsy}} and starts pacing.
drill.hint: unable to sit still (not *restless*, *fidgety*, *impatient* or *jittery*)

entries.related: *restless* — neutral; *fidgety* — moving small parts of your body; *on edge* — nervous and tense.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To suddenly start shouting angrily at someone or criticizing them harshly, often more than the situation deserves.
entries.usage: Common in casual American speech among all ages, and too casual for formal writing: *My boss went off on me in front of everyone.* It describes a sudden outburst that the speaker usually sees as unfair or too much. *Go off about* something means to rant about a topic, not at a person.
examples: My neighbor **went off on** me for parking two inches over his property line.
A customer **went off on** the cashier because the store was out of turkeys.
I asked my brother to turn down the music, and he totally **went off on** me.

drill.sentence: The coach {{went off on}} the referee after the bad call and got thrown out of the game.
drill.hint: suddenly shouted angrily at (not *yelled at*, *screamed at*, *tore into* or *laid into*)

entries.related: *lay into someone* — attack someone with words; *chew someone out* — scold someone angrily; *go off* (alone) — explode, or ring like an alarm.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To let out anger or frustration by talking about it, usually to someone who will just listen.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation and fine at work in a friendly tone: *Sorry, I just need to vent.* Use *vent to* + person and *vent about* + topic. The transitive form *vent your anger / frustration* is standard in any register.
examples: Sorry for the rant earlier; I just needed to **vent** about my in-laws.
She called her sister to **vent** about her terrible day at work.
Instead of yelling at the kids, I **vent** to my best friend on the phone after they're asleep.

drill.sentence: On our Friday walks, my neighbor and I {{vent}} about our teenagers and then feel much better.
drill.hint: let out our frustration by talking (not *rant*, *gripe* or *complain*)

entries.related: *rant* — speak angrily at length, sounds stronger; *let off steam* — release stress; *get something off your chest* — say something that has been bothering you.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To insult or criticize someone in a subtle, indirect way, often with a small comment or a look.
entries.usage: Slang made popular by the Black and Latino LGBTQ ballroom scene in New York, now common among younger speakers and in entertainment news. Use *throw shade at* + person; *shade* alone is the noun (*That was shade*). Too casual for work writing.
examples: She said my dress was "brave," which was definitely **throwing shade**.
The singer **threw shade** at her ex in her new song, and fans noticed immediately.
Was my mom **throwing shade** when she asked if I'd "finally" cleaned my room?

drill.sentence: When he said he'd "never pay that much for a car," he was {{throwing shade}} at my new SUV.
drill.hint: subtly insulting (slang; not *taking a dig* or *taking a shot*)

entries.related: *a dig* — a quiet critical remark; *diss* — slang, insult openly; *shady* (slang) — secretly unkind.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To make fun of someone harshly but humorously, usually in a friendly way and in front of others.
entries.usage: Used by all ages, especially younger people and on social media: *We roasted him all night.* It's the same idea as a *roast*, a comedy event where friends tell insulting jokes about a guest of honor. Among friends it's affectionate, but roasting someone you don't know well can feel like bullying.
examples: My friends **roasted** me all night about my new haircut.
At his retirement party, his coworkers **roasted** him about always being late.
My little sister **roasted** my outfit so hard that I went back and changed.

drill.sentence: The comments under my cooking video were brutal; people {{roasted}} me for burning the garlic.
drill.hint: made fun of me harshly, half as a joke (not *teased*, *mocked* or *dragged*)

entries.related: *tease* — neutral, gentler; *make fun of* — neutral, can be mean; *rib someone* — tease in a friendly way.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A remark that criticizes or mocks someone in a subtle or indirect way.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation and also in journalism about public arguments: *a dig at someone*, *take a dig at someone*, *Was that a dig?* It's more indirect than an open insult, so the speaker can often deny it. Informal but not slang, and fine in most settings except formal writing.
entries.pattern: a dig at someone; take / get in a dig
examples: When she thanked everyone "who showed up on time," it was clearly **a dig** at me.
His speech included a few **digs** at his former business partner.
"Nice of you to finally call." "Was that **a dig**?"

drill.sentence: My aunt said my apartment was "cozy for one," which felt like {{a dig}} at my love life.
drill.hint: a quietly critical remark (not *a jab*, *a swipe* or *a shot*)

entries.related: *a jab* — similar, sometimes more direct; *a backhanded compliment* — praise that hides criticism; *throw shade* — slang, insult subtly.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Sarcastic and mocking in a slightly rude or irritated way.
entries.usage: Common in casual speech and online, in both American and British English, about comments, emails, reviews and people: *a snarky reply*. It's critical but not very strong, and people often admit it about themselves (*Sorry, that was snarky*). The noun is *snark*, and both are too casual for formal writing.
examples: I asked a simple question, and he gave me a **snarky** answer about reading the manual.
My teenage son has been so **snarky** lately; every answer comes with an eye roll.
The restaurant's replies to bad reviews were so **snarky** that people started sharing them online.

drill.sentence: "Wow, you're only an hour late today," she said in a {{snarky}} tone.
drill.hint: sneering and a bit rude (not *sarcastic*, *snide*, *sassy* or *mocking*)

entries.related: *sarcastic* — neutral; *snide* — mean and indirect; *sassy* — cheeky, often in a fun way.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To claim something before anyone else can, like a seat, the last slice or the bigger room; *Dibs!* is what you shout.
entries.usage: Used in American speech mostly by kids, siblings and friends, but adults use it playfully too. The patterns are *call dibs on* + thing, *dibs on* + thing, or just *Dibs!* It's a game-like rule, so using it about serious things sounds childish or funny.
entries.pattern: call dibs on + thing; Dibs on + thing!
examples: "**Dibs on** the window seat!" my son shouted as soon as we got on the plane.
My roommate **called dibs on** the bigger bedroom before I even saw the apartment.
If nobody's eating that last slice of pizza, I'm **calling dibs**.

drill.sentence: We both wanted the bedroom with the ocean view, but my sister {{called dibs}} before we even unpacked.
drill.hint: made her claim first, playground style (two words; not *claimed it*)

entries.related: *call shotgun* — US, claim the front passenger seat of a car; *first come, first served* — whoever arrives first gets it; *claim* — neutral.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To bring bad luck to something, especially by talking about a good result before it happens (*Don't jinx it!*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, mostly as a half-joking warning: *Don't say that, you'll jinx it!* It works as a verb (*jinx it*) and a noun (*a jinx*, a person or thing that brings bad luck). Informal but not slang; American kids also shout *Jinx!* when two people say the same thing at once.
examples: Don't say we're going to win; you'll **jinx** it!
I didn't tell anyone about the job offer because I didn't want to **jinx** it.
Our flight is actually on time for once. Oh no, I probably just **jinxed** it.

drill.sentence: "The baby's been sleeping through the night all week!" "Shh, don't {{jinx}} it!"
drill.hint: bring bad luck to (not *curse* or *ruin*)

entries.related: *knock on wood* — US phrase said to avoid bad luck (British *touch wood*); *curse* — stronger, magical; *tempt fate* — take a risk by being too confident.

entries.label: phrasal verb
entries.meaning: To go somewhere with someone, often without being invited or as an extra person in their plans.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech: *Mind if I tag along?* is a polite, modest way to ask to join. Use *tag along with* + person. Said about someone else, it can suggest they weren't really invited (*His little brother always tags along*).
examples: You're going to the farmers market? Mind if I **tag along**?
My little sister always **tagged along** when I went out with my friends.
I **tagged along** to my wife's work dinner and ended up having a great time.

drill.sentence: We're getting ice cream after the game; you're welcome to {{tag along}} if you want.
drill.hint: go with us as an extra person (not *join us*; the verb is not *come*)

entries.related: *come along* — neutral, often invited; *join someone* — neutral; *a third wheel* — an extra person with a couple.

entries.label: verb
entries.meaning: To spend time casually with someone, without a special plan (*We should hang sometime*).
entries.usage: Slang that is very common among younger Americans and in texts; it's a shorter form of *hang out*. Use *hang* alone (*Want to hang?*) or *hang with* + person. Older speakers usually say *hang out*, which is informal but not slang.
examples: We should **hang** sometime; I feel like I never see you anymore.
I'm just **hanging with** my cousins at the lake this weekend.
"What are you doing tonight?" "Nothing much, just **hanging** at home."

drill.sentence: "Want to {{hang}} this weekend?" "Sure, I'm free Saturday afternoon."
drill.hint: spend time together casually (slang, one word; not *chill* or *meet up*)

entries.related: *hang out* — informal, not slang; *chill* — slang, relax together; *a hang* — slang noun, a casual get-together.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To like each other immediately and get along well when you first meet.
entries.usage: Used by all ages about friends, couples, coworkers and even pets: *We hit it off right away.* The subject is usually plural (*They hit it off*), or you use *hit it off with* + person. It's always positive and fine in most settings except formal writing.
entries.pattern: A and B hit it off; hit it off with someone
examples: My mom and my girlfriend **hit it off** right away; now they text each other more than I do.
I sat next to a stranger on the flight, and we **hit it off** so well that we're meeting for coffee next week.
The two dogs **hit it off** at the park and played for an hour.

drill.sentence: I was nervous about meeting my new roommate, but we {{hit it off}} over our shared love of terrible horror movies.
drill.hint: liked each other instantly (not *clicked*, *bonded* or *got along*)

entries.related: *click* — informal, same idea; *get along* — have a good relationship over time; *bond* — become close.

entries.label: informal phrase
entries.meaning: To be attracted to someone, often secretly or in a way you haven't acted on yet.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, often in gossip or teasing: *I think he has a thing for you.* It's lighter than *be in love with* and usually means a crush that hasn't been acted on. *Have a thing for* + thing means a special liking (*a thing for old cars*).
examples: I'm pretty sure Sam **has a thing for** you; he laughs at all your jokes.
In high school, I **had a huge thing for** my best friend's older brother.
She's always **had a thing for** guys with accents.

drill.sentence: Everyone can tell that Dan {{has a thing for}} his neighbor; he blushes whenever she waves.
drill.hint: is secretly attracted to (not *has a crush on*, *likes* or *is into*)

entries.related: *have a crush on* — very close, a bit more youthful; *be into someone* — be attracted to them; *have feelings for* — more serious.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Unreliable: often canceling plans, forgetting promises or not showing up.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual American speech about friends, dates, contractors and coworkers: *He's a little flaky.* It describes a pattern, so it's real criticism of someone's character. A *flake* is a flaky person, and *flake on* + person is the verb.
examples: I love Jenna, but she's so **flaky**; she's canceled on me three times this month.
Our last plumber was really **flaky**, so this time we're hiring a bigger company.
Don't be **flaky**; if you say you'll be there at eight, be there at eight.

drill.sentence: I stopped making plans with Chris because he's too {{flaky}}; he never shows up when he says he will.
drill.hint: always canceling or forgetting plans (not *unreliable*)

entries.related: *unreliable* — neutral; *a flake* — a flaky person; *dependable* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: A person who doesn't come although they were expected, for example to a meeting, appointment, reservation or flight.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation and also in business, travel and medical settings, where it's almost a technical term (*a no-show fee*, *the no-show rate*). It's informal but neutral enough for work emails. As a verb, *no-show* is more casual: *Half the guests no-showed.*
examples: We booked a table for eight, but three people were **no-shows**.
The dentist charges fifty dollars if you're **a no-show** without calling.
The star player was **a no-show** at practice, and the coach benched him for the next game.

drill.sentence: The plumber was supposed to come at nine, but he was {{a no-show}} and didn't even call.
drill.hint: a person who never turned up (not *absent* or *late*)

entries.related: *stand someone up* — not come to a date or meeting; *flake* — fail to show up, often repeatedly; *absent* — neutral, not present.

entries.label: noun
entries.meaning: Someone who needs to control everything and everyone around them and finds it hard to let others decide.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation about bosses, partners, parents and roommates. It's critical, but people often say it about themselves with humor (*I'm a bit of a control freak about the kitchen*). Too blunt for a work email or a performance review.
examples: My old boss was a total **control freak**; she rewrote every email I sent.
I'll admit I'm a bit of a **control freak** when it comes to planning vacations.
He's such **a control freak** that nobody else is allowed to touch the TV remote.

drill.sentence: My roommate plans every detail of our weekends and gets upset if we change anything; she's a real {{control freak}}.
drill.hint: someone who must be in charge of everything (not *perfectionist* or *planner*)

entries.related: *micromanager* — a boss who controls every small detail; *perfectionist* — wants everything perfect; *bossy* — likes telling others what to do.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Needing a lot of attention, effort, care or money to keep happy or in good condition.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation about people, pets, plants, cars and hair: *a high-maintenance friend*. About a person it's critical, suggesting they're demanding or fussy. Hyphenate it before a noun; after *be*, people write it with or without the hyphen.
examples: Orchids are beautiful, but they're way too **high-maintenance** for me.
Her ex was really **high-maintenance**; every date had to be at a fancy restaurant.
We wanted a dog that wasn't too **high-maintenance**, so we skipped breeds that need daily grooming.

drill.sentence: My car is so {{high-maintenance}} that I spend more on repairs than on gas.
drill.hint: needing lots of care and money (not *needy* or *demanding*)

entries.related: *low-maintenance* — the opposite, easy to deal with; *needy* — needing a lot of emotional attention; *fussy* — hard to please.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Tense and anxious, and often too strict, formal or easily offended to relax.
entries.usage: Used by all ages in casual speech, usually as a criticism: *Don't be so uptight.* It can describe a mood (*He's uptight about the move*) or a person's character (*an uptight neighbor*). Saying it to someone's face can sound rude, so be careful outside close friends.
examples: My neighbor is so **uptight** that he complains if our music is on after eight.
I get a little **uptight** before flights, so I don't talk much at the airport.
Everyone was **uptight** at the first rehearsal, but the director's jokes helped.

drill.sentence: Relax, it's just a picnic. You don't need to be so {{uptight}} about the seating plan.
drill.hint: nervous and rigid (not *stressed*, *tense*, *fussy* or *worked up*)

entries.related: *laid-back* — the opposite, relaxed; *tense* — neutral, nervous; *stuck-up* — arrogant, a different idea.

entries.label: adjective
entries.meaning: Cheap-looking, showy or in poor taste; also socially inappropriate (*It's tacky to ask about money*).
entries.usage: Used by all ages in conversation about clothes, decorations, gifts and behavior: *tacky souvenirs*, *a tacky comment*. It judges taste or manners, so saying it about someone's choices can sound snobbish or rude. *Tacky* also means slightly sticky (*The paint is still tacky*), a separate, neutral sense.
examples: The hotel lobby was full of **tacky** gold statues and fake palm trees.
Is it **tacky** to ask for cash instead of wedding gifts?
Her uncle showed up in a **tacky** Hawaiian shirt covered in pink flamingos.

drill.sentence: Leaving the price tag on a gift is kind of {{tacky}}, don't you think?
drill.hint: showing bad taste or manners (not *tasteless*, *cheap* or *rude*)

entries.related: *cheesy* — sentimental or cheap-looking; *gaudy* — too bright and showy; *classy* — the opposite.
